ratings_why.fun: Feeding one crowned bird on a cleared lek is a story you can see grow, but every duel asks you to work out a quarter of two sums, and Pilgrim with Cantor makes a lot of arithmetic per refresh.
ratings_why.distinct: One verb used in three places, empty slots as power, and losing on purpose to buy the winner don't play like today's tribes or like a generic buff tribe.

verdict_why: Grit Pit Elder and Cantor still don't read cleanly; both are short wording fixes, and the rest of the tribe can stay as it is.

points.text: Grit Pit Elder says permanently and Four times a turn, but most duels happen in fights. Say whether fight duels count, and whether a fight win gives a permanent gain.

Cantor names other cards in its text and uses "chain" without defining it. Something like "When one of your units duels several in a row, each duel repeats before the next" reads without the names. Also say whether Ottokar's stop check applies to the repeat.
Lord of the Old Lek carries two unrelated rules. The rule that empty slots count as survivors could sit on its own card, so each card reads as one idea.
The fantasy lands best where empty space matters (Prior, Lord). Hartmut could show the deafness too, for example by ignoring the first effect that would shrink or move him.

standouts.why: Prior of the Needle Refectory: an empty slot next to the champion is the lek itself, and you can read it on the board at a glance.
Squire Konrad loses to the elder and grows from it. The card is the yearling at the edge of the lek.
Dame Reisig is the judging hen with a real job: she pays for wins and rewards buying the shop unit that beat you.

weakest.why: Cantor of the Whetting Song is the hardest card to read, and doubling every duel doubles the math a player has to track.
Grit Pit Elder is a plain counter on duel wins, and its limit and timing are unclear.
Keeper of the Gizzard Stones reads clearly but has no picture of its own beyond a bigger number.

flags.note: Its limit counts per turn and its gain is permanent, so it's unclear whether fight duels trigger it.
Its chain wording leans on card names, and it's unclear whether Ottokar's stop check applies to repeats.
With Keeper and Cantor, Pilgrim takes from the whole shop three times a turn: the design flags this itself.
